description: From orbit to the farm: ORYZON brings NASA data down to Philippine fields. Six Electronics and Communications Engineering students from the University of the Philippines Diliman, bound by a love of space, are focusing their efforts on rice (Oryza sativa), the staple food of their country. Using research, programming, data analysis, and data visualization, they turn NASA’s view from orbit into practical help for the people who feed the country.
summary: ORYZON is a website application that turns NASA Earth observations into clear decisions for rice farmers. Upon launching the website, the farmer will be asked to outline their field on a satellite map, and ORYZON averages NASA temperature, rainfall, and soil-moisture data over that exact polygon. It compares each reading with the area's own history and reports it as a Good / Watch / Alert status. Using DSSAT crop simulations, it then ranks the top three crops or rice varieties to plant next by comparing their expected yields, and shows the soil's net change in carbon and nitrogen. Through this web app, farmers can see the effects of specific crops on their own field and learn why rotation matters.
details:
1. Project Description

The problem. 

In the Philippines, rice farmers face less predictable rain, dry-season water shortages, typhoons, and declining soil health, yet most plant rice season after season. Hence the concept of rotation comes in. Rotation is known locally but rarely adopted, and farmers from rural areas have little access to field-level data.

What ORYZON does.

  • Farm Outlining. Tap the corners of the field on a satellite basemap. A built-in land check rejects outlines that are mostly open water, and place search jumps the map to any location.
  • Farm Set Up. Add plots drawn inside the farm, previous crop records with planting and harvest dates, yields and performance, and water availability (rain-fed, irrigation, or both). Farm records stay on the farmer's device.
  • Read the dashboard. Temperature, soil moisture, and rainfall each get a status with a plain explanation, such as "Dry spell: 7.2 mm in the last 14 days," and an "as of" date. Heat-map layers and a day slider show how conditions change across the region. History charts, a plot ring chart, and a harvest-by-season chart summarize the farm.
  • Educate. The Crop Guide covers seven crops (maize, potato, soybean, cabbage, tomato, sugarcane, dry bean) with growing periods and their effects on soil.
  • Plan for next season. The farmer chooses what to plant next: planting rice again or another crop before rice. ORYZON returns the top three options, each as a percentage of its ideal yield with a range, along with the soil net change over the run.

2. How It Works

  • Front end: React, TypeScript, Vite, and Leaflet. The map is always the background and every screen is an overlay on it, so the field stays in view.
  • NASA data backend (FastAPI): It serves as NASA POWER daily temperature and corrected precipitation and FLDAS monthly soil moisture (0–10 cm). For each layer it provides a color-coded heat map per day and the daily average over the farmer's polygon. Fill values are masked before averaging. Monthly layers repeat across the days of the month so every layer fits one slider.
  • Status engine: Each reading is ranked against the area's own history and checked against stress rules for heat, extreme rain, dry spells, and unusually dry or waterlogged soil. The result is a Good, Watch, or Alert status that needs no training data. Every status is explainable, and the thresholds can be measured per crop stage.
  • DSSAT recommendation service: For each candidate rice variety or yield crop, it runs an actual and an ideal CERES-Rice simulation from the farm's location, planting date, and chosen pre-crop. Candidates are ranked by mean percent of ideal yield, so a long-season and a short-season crop can be compared fairly. Sequenced runs pass the resulting soil state (water, nitrate, ammonium) into the next crop. Yields of different crops are never added together.
  • Handling data of different resolutions: Layers are masked, aligned in time, and averaged over the polygon. Each value is labeled with its date and as a regional estimate, because a NASA grid cell covers more than one farm.
  • Privacy by design: Farm records never leave the device. The data backend receives only the polygon, and the simulation service receives only the farm's center point and a few choices.

3. Benefits and Goals

ORYZON gives a farmer field-level evidence in simplified terms, with no GIS or data skills needed. It puts non-rice options such as crops beside the current practice of planting rice again, so the benefits of rotation (nitrogen for the next crop, lower water use, broken pest cycles, healthier soil) can be seen in numbers. Every result provides reliable approximations of weather scenarios, crop recommendations, and projected yield with is expected income. The goal is to raise rotation adoption and make rice farms more resilient to a changing climate.

4. Alignment with the Challenge

ORYZON combines NASA Earth observations with crop characteristics and the farmer's own records to compare three rotation strategies, including the farmer's existing one (rice). It explains why options rank as they do through percent of ideal yield and soil changes. It also shows uncertainty through yield ranges, expected growth rates, recommendation notes, leaving the farmer as the ultimate decision maker.

5. Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini were used as assistants for drafting text, explaining DSSAT and NASA datasets, and suggesting or reviewing code. The team designed, ran, and tested the application and is responsible for its content. No AI generated or altered the satellite data. The app calls no AI model at run time: its statuses come from fixed rules and its recommendations from DSSAT simulations.
